nuggets.title: Late Bulk Upload Rewrites Historical Rollups Wrong

scenario.symptoms: Temperature charts show impossible spikes after devices reconnect; hourly rollups double-count late batches.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Rollup jobs treat ingestion time as event time and append instead of upserting by device event timestamp.

incident.headline: Ingestion-time rollups corrupt charts when events arrive late

agenda.goal: Place late and out-of-order readings correctly and update derived data.
agenda.opener: A device is offline for hours, then uploads everything at once. What happens to its charts and rollups?

evidence.strong: Keys readings by device time and sequence, writes raw points idempotently, recomputes only the affected rollup windows, keeps live views from going backwards, and bounds lateness so stragglers go through a batch correction.
evidence.adequate: Stores late readings but never updates rollups, or reprocesses everything.
evidence.weak: Stamps readings with arrival time, so a day of readings lands in one minute.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks using the time a reading arrives is good enough.
misconceptions.challenge: A day's buffered readings arrive in one burst. What does the device's chart look like?

probes: How do you avoid storing the same reading twice if the upload is retried?
Which rollups need recomputing, and how do you find them?
hints: The reading's own timestamp and sequence say where it belongs.
Only windows that received new points need recomputing.
agenda.referenceFix: Event-time placement with sequence-number dedupe, idempotent raw writes and recomputation of only the affected rollup windows.

scenario.symptoms: Dashboard year-view queries exceed 60s timeout; raw 1-second samples scanned for single device chart.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Long-range queries hit raw high-resolution table without downsampled tier or pre-aggregated rollups.

incident.headline: Missing downsampling tier makes long-range charts non-viable

agenda.goal: Serve long-range charts fast with downsampled data and keep storage proportional.
agenda.opener: How do you serve a one-year chart for one device in under a second?

evidence.strong: Precomputes rollups (min, max, average, count per minute and per hour) as readings arrive, queries the coarsest resolution that fits the range, and uses columnar compression; raw data expires after its retention period.
evidence.adequate: Mentions downsampling but computes it at query time or keeps only averages.
evidence.weak: Reads every raw point for the year at query time.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes storing only averages is enough for rollups.
misconceptions.challenge: A pressure spike lasts ten seconds. Does an hourly average show it?

probes: Which statistics would you keep per bucket?
How does the query choose a resolution?
hints: A chart only has so many pixels.
Keep more than the mean so spikes stay visible.
agenda.referenceFix: Precomputed multi-resolution rollups with min, max, average and count, chosen by query range.

nuggets.title: Regional Power Restore Triggers Ingestion Storm

scenario.symptoms: After outage, 200k devices reconnect within 60s; ingest gateway returns 503 and drops telemetry batches.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Devices upload full offline backlog immediately with no jitter; gateway has fixed connection limits.

incident.headline: Mass reconnect without backoff overwhelms ingest tier

agenda.goal: Survive a mass reconnect after a regional outage.
agenda.opener: A power cut ends and a huge number of devices reconnect within a minute, each uploading a backlog. What protects the pipeline?

evidence.strong: Devices reconnect with randomised exponential backoff; gateways admit connections at a controlled rate and push back; the log absorbs the burst, consumers catch up with autoscaling, and live data is prioritised over backlog.
evidence.adequate: Scales the gateways but ignores client backoff or prioritisation.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks autoscaling alone absorbs a reconnect storm.
misconceptions.challenge: New gateway instances take minutes to start. What happens to the devices connecting in the first minute?

probes: Should backlog uploads compete with live readings?
hints: Clients can spread their own retries out.
A durable log lets you accept fast and process later.
agenda.referenceFix: Jittered backoff on devices, rate-limited admission at gateways, the log as a buffer, and live data before backlog.

nuggets.title: Drifted Device Clocks Scatter Metrics on Timeline

scenario.symptoms: Fleet dashboard shows future-dated readings and negative durations; alerting misfires on clock-skewed devices.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Server trusts device-reported timestamps without skew detection or server-side normalization.

incident.headline: Uncorrected device clock skew corrupts time-series ordering

agenda.goal: Handle device clocks that are wrong.
agenda.opener: A device's clock is well off. What does that do to your data, and how do you handle it?

evidence.strong: Stores device time, server receive time and sequence; estimates skew per device from receive time on live readings, corrects or flags readings, rejects impossible timestamps, and keeps raw values for audit.
evidence.adequate: Replaces device time with server time, losing correct offline timestamps.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes overwriting device time with server receive time fixes skew.
misconceptions.challenge: A device uploads yesterday's buffered readings now. What timestamps do they get?

probes: How would you even detect that a clock is wrong?
hints: Compare the device's time with when you received live readings.
Keep both timestamps rather than choosing one.
agenda.referenceFix: Keep device time, receive time and sequence; estimate and correct skew per device and flag bad timestamps.

nuggets.title: Silent Devices Not Detected Within SLA

scenario.symptoms: Critical freezer sensors stop reporting for 45 minutes before anyone notices; SLA requires 1-minute detection.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Alerting evaluates threshold rules only on incoming points with no heartbeat or absence detection.

incident.headline: Missing absence detection delays silent device alerts

agenda.goal: Evaluate threshold rules and detect silent devices within a minute.
agenda.opener: How do you notice that a device has stopped reporting, and how do threshold alerts fire quickly?

evidence.strong: Evaluates rules in the stream per device with keyed state, deduplicates and debounces alerts, and detects silence with a per-device timer that fires when no reading arrives within the expected interval; sends to a notification service.
evidence.adequate: Fires threshold alerts in the stream but detects silence with a periodic database scan.
evidence.weak: Checks alerts by querying the database every few minutes for every device.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks scanning all devices periodically is the way to find silent ones.
misconceptions.challenge: Scanning millions of devices every minute: what does that cost, and how fast is it?

probes: How do you stop one flapping sensor from sending hundreds of alerts?
hints: Absence of data is an event you can schedule a timer for.
Debounce alerts that flip on and off.
agenda.referenceFix: Stream-side rule evaluation with keyed state, per-device timers for silence, and debounced notifications.
